chapter_theme: The mullai fifty's first decade: after the prefatory verse, the friend and the waiting wife read the rainy season, its cloud, thunder, jasmine and the herdsman's evening flute, as his promised return or as an assault on her alone (1-9); then the husband, returning, hurries his chariot to see her waiting (10).

payiram.reading: The prefatory verse says that Maran Poraiyan of generous fame bound together the Ainthinai Aimpathu so that great men of good character might see its worth, and that those who do not recite it with eagerness have not attained pure Tamil.
payiram.nuance: It praises a book, not a king, and makes the fifty poems a test of belonging to செந்தமிழ்: the five landscapes are offered as the curriculum of correct Tamil, not only as love poetry.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the poet and his book, the nearest puram class to a eulogy

1.reading: Good lady, the friend says, see: the rain cloud has gathered, massed and dark like the colour of Mal who overcame the wrestlers, flashing with lightning that is the spear of Murugan who wears the kadamba, making the konrai bloom as the garland of Shiva who shot the moving forts, and it rises turning to the right.
1.nuance: Three gods each lend the storm one attribute: Mal, god of the mullai, its colour; Murugan, god of the hills, its lightning; Shiva its konrai. The cloud rising on the right (வலன் ஏரும்) is the auspicious omen, so the friend shows the season as a sacred sign of his return rather than only as weather.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud rising on the right fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the konrai blossoms, as Shiva's garland

2.reading: As the beautiful peacock calls, the roaring sky, which has taken on the nature of rain, thunders and hangs low over the sapphire-dark mountain; every time she sees it, the heroine tells her soft-spoken friend, her shoulders take on the yellow of the peerkku flower.
2.nuance: The two halves are built on the same phrase: the sky takes on the nature of rain (கார்நீர்மை கொண்ட) and her shoulders take on the nature of the peerkku (பீர்நீர்மை கொண்டன), so the season's fulfilment and her pallor arrive as one event. The speaker could also be the friend observing the heroine's shoulders; the vocative பணிமொழி fits either.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-laden roaring sky and the calling peacock fix the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders turned the yellow of the peerkku flower, the pallor of separation

3.reading: Lightning, thunder and the thunderbolt, such killing weapons this rain has spread wide; she asks her friend, whose teeth outshine jasmine buds, whether there is no such rain in the land where their man has gone.
3.nuance: The question is an accusation turned inside out: if the rain were in his land too, he would have read it and come, so either it is not there or he has not heeded it. The season meant to be his signal falls on her alone as an attacking army.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season's lightning and thunder and the jasmine

comparisons.tenor: lightning, thunder and thunderbolt, as an army's killing weapons
the friend's teeth, which surpass jasmine buds in whiteness

4.reading: Does our lover not think of how it is with us, she asks her bright-bangled friend: this rain, roaring like the voice of a strapped war-drum and appearing so as to seize the hearts of good women, has grown keen as if to kill the soft-spoken one.
4.nuance: The war-drum makes the thunder a summons to battle aimed at women (நல்லார் மனங்கவர), and the soft-spoken one it would kill is the speaker herself named in the third person; it may instead be the friend speaking of the heroine.

thinai_evidence.note: the roaring rain cloud fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the rain cloud
the rain grown sharp as a weapon meant to kill

5.reading: Each time she sees the sky, where dark clouds gather on the high-peaked mountain, spread in rows with their heads tangling, run on mingled with the wind and pour down, her eyes fall too, mingled with drops.
5.nuance: The verbs carry over: what the clouds do in three lines (கலந்து, வந்து உறைக்கும்) her eyes do in one (துளிகலந்து வீழ்தரும்), so the poem never says 'I weep like the rain' but makes her tears another fall of the same storm.

thinai_evidence.note: the massed rain clouds pouring fix the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, which pour drops as the clouds do

6.reading: The dark bee humming after sipping the fragrant jasmine is sweet to those who have someone to lean on, she tells her good friend, but on us, who live with hearts that have no one, the dark evening comes and saws.
6.nuance: The same hour is sweet or cruel by company alone (செல்சார்வு உடையார்க்கு), so the evening's cruelty is in her solitude. The bee at the jasmine is a near miss for iraicchi: it acts like a lover, but the poem itself states the contrast, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the jasmine and the darkening evening, mullai's flower and hour

comparisons.tenor: the evening that cuts her as a saw cuts

7.reading: In the dull evening when the sun has hidden behind the hill and the sky holds its red glow, the sound of the fine little flute the herdsman plays in joy once the cattle have fed, she tells her friend of close-set bangles, is to her like a spear thrown at her.
7.nuance: The herdsman plays because he is glad (உவந்து ஊதும்) and his flute is called fine (சீர்சால்): the music is not harsh, it wounds because it announces a homecoming that is not hers.

thinai_evidence.note: the red evening and the herdsman's flute, mullai's hour and people

comparisons.tenor: the herdsman's flute, which strikes her like a thrown spear

8.reading: The valli creeper, dull like the bodies of those who are parted, has grown lovely like the bodies of those united; she asks her well-adorned friend whether, even though the sky now pours, the man who crossed the cruel forest will not come.
8.nuance: The usual direction of the simile is reversed: human bodies are the vehicle and the plant the tenor. The creeper has passed from the parted state to the united one; she has not, so the plant shows her the change the season promised her.

thinai_evidence.note: the pouring rain that revives the creeper fixes the rainy season

comparisons.tenor: the creeper as it was before the rain, dull
the creeper revived by the rain, lovely

9.reading: He will come, the friend tells the heroine of shining jewels; she need not melt and waste away with her bright sword-like eyes full of tears: if she will look, the green-stemmed jasmine has put forth opening buds, having heard the secret of the new rain.
9.nuance: The jasmine is said to have heard the secret (மறை) of the coming rain before anyone saw it, so the friend offers it as inside knowledge of the season. It is a near miss for iraicchi: the flower's answering of the season's message suggests the man will answer too, but it is offered as evidence, not as an act a person of the situation does, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the jasmine in bud is mullai's flower and the sign of its season

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, bright and sharp as a sword

10.reading: Charioteer skilled by the rule, the returning man says, let the chariot go swiftly; looking at the beauty of the forest where bees hum, let us learn the state of her who stands with the bolt of her practised chastity drawn shut and her hand pressed to her cheek.
10.nuance: Chastity is a door bar she has let fall, so her waiting is a house closed from within; the hand on the cheek is the posture of that waiting. He wants to see her before she sees him, to know her state as it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest road home by chariot, the mullai land of the returning husband

comparisons.tenor: her chastity, as a bolt dropped to shut the house

links.note: Kar Narpathu 12: the dark clouds, like oiled elephants, rise on the right every day (ஏரும் வலம்), a sign beyond doubt. Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 ends on the same omen, வலனேருங் கார், after giving the cloud the colour of Mal, the spear of Murugan and the garland of Shiva.
links.teaches: The rightward rise is a fixed reassurance in the mullai venba, and holding the two together shows the Ainthinai poet strengthening a plain omen by assembling three gods' emblems around it, where Kar Narpathu leans on its daily regularity.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 1 makes the rainbow the garland on the chest of sea-coloured Mal; Ainthinai Aimpathu 1 gives Mal the cloud's dark body and gives the garland to Shiva as the konrai.
links.teaches: Both opening verses of the mullai collections divine the storm, but they share it out differently, so the god of the mullai was a ready frame that each poet filled by choosing which part of the sky belongs to which god.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4: the friend calls the season, with peacocks and konrai, the medicine for the heroine's wasting pallor. Ainthinai Aimpathu 2: with the peacock calling and the rain cloud low, every sight of the sky turns the heroine's shoulders yellow. On a plain reading the same season cures the pallor and causes it.
links.teaches: Set side by side the friend's argument and the heroine's experience disagree about the same sky, which shows that the season-as-proof consolation works only from outside, while to the waiting woman the season itself is the illness.

links.note: Natrinai 69: if the evening came like this in the land where he went for work, he could not hold to his resolve. Ainthinai Aimpathu 3: is there not this rain in the land where our man went?
links.teaches: The pair shows a single argument of the waiting wife, that the season must reach him too and would bring him home, carried from evening in the long poem to the rain in the venba, where its failure becomes the sharper doubt whether the rain is in his land at all.

links.note: Kural 1224: when the lover is absent, evening comes like enemies to a killing ground. Ainthinai Aimpathu 6: evening, sweet with the bee at the jasmine for those who have company, comes and saws those who have no one.
links.teaches: Both women make evening a killer, but the venba adds that the same hour is sweet to the companioned, so it locates the couplet's hostility in the absence and not in evening itself, which the couplet's 'when the lover is absent' only implies.

links.note: Kural 1228: the herdsman's flute, envoy of the burning evening, is a weapon that kills. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7: at red evening the herdsman's fine little flute, played in joy once the cattle have fed, is to her like a spear thrown.
links.teaches: The couplet states that the flute is a deadly weapon, and the venba supplies the scene that explains it: the herdsman plays for joy at his own day's return, so the weapon is someone else's homecoming.

links.note: Akananuru 74: the heroine could hold firm on her friend's comfort if the hard-mouthed small flute (வல்வாய் சிறுகுழல்) of the unlettered herdsmen did not torment her in the evening. Ainthinai Aimpathu 7 calls the same small flute fine (சீர்சால் சிறுகுழல்) and its player glad, yet it strikes her like a spear.
links.teaches: One heroine blames the flute's harsh mouth and the other concedes its sweetness, so together they show the evening flute's pain moving from the instrument to the hearer, which is why the venba needs the simile of the spear.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 18: the forest, dull like the body of a poor man, has put forth beauty like a rich man's mind. Ainthinai Aimpathu 8: the valli, dull like the body of the parted, has grown lovely like the body of the united.
links.teaches: Both measure the revived plant by a human state, but Kar Narpathu uses poverty and wealth, the motive of his journey, and Ainthinai uses parting and union, its outcome, so the same simile can point either to why he left or to what she awaits.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 14: the friend is sure he will come quickly, since the cool rain cloud laughs softly as the jasmine shows its bright teeth. Ainthinai Aimpathu 9: he will come; the jasmine has opened its buds, having heard the secret of the new rain.
links.teaches: In both the friend's proof is the budding jasmine, but one reads it as the season's laughter and the other as the season's whispered secret already received, so the same flower serves as a public sign in one and as private knowledge in the other.

links.note: Natrinai 142: returning, the man tells his charioteer of the young woman of mullai-fitting chastity who rejoices when a guest comes even at night. Ainthinai Aimpathu 10: returning, he tells the charioteer to hurry to see her who stands with the bolt of her chastity drawn shut, hand to cheek.
links.teaches: The same speaker on the same road imagines the wife's chastity as an open door to guests in one poem and as a shut bolt in the other, so the pair shows karpu as both the household's hospitality and its closing against the world while the husband is away.

source_issues: Verse 10: show flags that sangamtamil.com's text lacks line 1 (நூல்நின்ற பாக! தேர் நொவ்விதாச் சென்றீக); our text has all four lines.
Verse 1 line 3 எய்தவன தார் and verse 7 line 3 சிறுகுழல ஓசை look like எய்தவன் தார் and சிறுகுழல் ஓசை with the final consonant misprinted; the sense is unaffected.
Bracketed sandhi letters are printed in the text (மற்(று), கொண்(டு), கூர்ந்த(து), அரும்(பு)); words cited from them omit the brackets.
The colophons give no thurai for any verse of this chapter, so thurai_akam speakers are inferred from the verses and occasion words are null.
